title: Political Dexterity: The Capability That Decides What Survives
author: Colin Gautrey
summary: Colin Gautrey argues that the primary reason well-funded, well-staffed transformation efforts fail is not process, budget, or commitment but the absence of a specific, rarely-named capability he calls 'political dexterity' -- the ability to move a complex human system toward an outcome it would not reach on its own. He describes how organizational resistance to change is structural rather than personal: systems protect their own coherence, and what looks like stalling (requests for more evidence, competing priorities, budgets quietly disappearing) is the system behaving predictably, not a setback that more pressure will fix. Gautrey's sharpest claim is diagnostic: decades of change-management methodology have never addressed this capability gap because executive competency frameworks talk around it using safer language (organizational savvy, stakeholder management) rather than naming the discomforting word 'politics' directly, which leaves most senior professionals underdeveloped in exactly the capability their situation most demands. He defines political dexterity as operating on two inseparable levels -- an accurate, continuous reading of where power actually flows, and the judgment to act on that reading at the right moment -- and argues that formal authority is commonly mistaken for a substitute for it, an error that compounds silently. The essay closes by distinguishing political dexterity from manipulation: at its most developed, it produces change that becomes the system's own logic rather than something imposed and merely complied with, which Gautrey calls transformative leadership at its highest expression.
points: Gautrey's core diagnostic reframes change-management failure: adequately funded, seriously staffed initiatives still fail because none of the standard tools address the specific capability of moving a system toward an outcome it wouldn't reach on its own -- a gap process alone cannot close.

His account of why the capability goes undeveloped is a naming problem, not a competence problem: executive frameworks use safer synonyms (organisational savvy, stakeholder management) because the word 'politics' triggers discomfort, and an unnamed capability cannot be assessed or deliberately developed.

He gives leaders a concrete diagnostic for misreading resistance: signals like requests for more evidence or a project quietly losing its budget are not setbacks to push harder against -- they are the system behaving normally, and added pressure produces more sophisticated resistance, not compliance.

His closing distinction -- that political dexterity's highest expression makes the operator redundant to the outcome they set in motion, because the change becomes the system's own logic -- offers a concrete test for whether a change effort has actually landed versus merely been complied with.
quotes: What is missing is the capability to move a complex human system toward an outcome it would not reach on its own. That capability has a name. Almost nobody has had the courage to use it. It is called political dexterity.
They are not setbacks. They are the system behaving naturally. Applying more pressure to a system behaving naturally does not produce different results. It produces more sophisticated resistance.

The research has been clear for years that political capability is among the primary determinants of whether significant change lands or fails. Most serious studies of change failure point to political resistance as the dominant cause.

The cultural discomfort that prevents organisations from naming political dexterity plainly is the same discomfort that ensures most of their senior people remain underdeveloped in the one capability their situation now most demands.
The senior professional who reads the system accurately but cannot act on what they see achieves clarity without impact. The one who acts without reading generates effort without traction.

They shape conditions until the system completes the journey without them. The change embeds. The new direction becomes the system's own logic. The operator becomes redundant to the outcome they set in motion.
